text:
白天刚在法庭上输掉与 OpenAI 的百亿对决，当晚马斯克坐在福布斯晚宴上，状态失神的让人心疼，但他却说出了全场最让人脊背发凉的一句话：
AI 在全方位超越人类，大概只剩一两年，连创新这种人类最后的自尊，马上也要被彻底端平了。

马斯克这个大帅比真的牛逼，在输掉了一场关乎全球最大 AI 资产控制权的官司之后，他没有把时间浪费在抱怨法官或对手身上，而是用一种罕见的失神状态讲出了这番话：

“我对 AI 既惊恐又兴奋，AI 在各方面超越人类，大概不出一两年。”

很多人看热闹，总以为这只是一次商业巨头败诉后的公关失态，或者又一次习惯性的技术恐吓。

但如果我们把败诉这个残酷的现实切口拼上去，就会发现这其实是一个顶级操盘手在亲手被踢下棋盘后，吐出的一句绝望真话：
当创造者自己都被商业机制和法律条文剥夺了对 AI 舵盘的掌控权时，连世界首富也不得不面对现实——
人类这个物种，正在以天为单位，快速滑向丧失全面主导权的边缘。

在过去的认知里，人类总喜欢把最后一张自尊的底牌压在“创新”和“灵性”上。

大家觉得算力再强也只能模仿套路，机器只能消化人类喂给它的旧数据，真正的逻辑跃迁、底层发明和灵光一闪，永远属于肉身大脑。

但在专访里，马斯克彻底敲碎了这个自欺欺人的遮羞布：
AI 在全方位碾压人类，不仅包含算力、记忆和体力，更包含了人类最引以为傲的“无中生有”的发明与创新能力。

每天都在爆发的算法突破，连站在全球算力最前沿的人都感到头晕目眩。
当创新本身被转化成一种以光速自我演进的高维算法时，肉身科学家的迭代速度，在它面前慢得就像地质纪元里的冰川。

更刺骨的是，面对这种全方位的智力降维打击，马斯克最终收敛成了一句近乎无力的祈祷：
“我希望它对我们友好。”
以前的商业战争，输了可以重组资本、招募团队，在下一个周期杀回来。

但 AI 时代的游戏规则完全变了：
一旦智能的代际差距拉大到无法逾越的断层，人类之间为了权力和控制权而打的每一场官司，在未来那个冷酷的超级智能眼里，都轻得像一群蚂蚁为了面包屑打架。

所以我们别再争论谁在这场官司里赢了名誉和金钱，
当裁判哨声吹响的时候，场上的两位棋手可能都还没意识到：
那个在棋盘深处不断被喂大的造物，已经快要站起身来，把整张桌子掀掉了。
author: AYi_AInotes
quoted_text:
马斯克第一次公开正面回应了跟@OpenAI 诉讼案的核心实质以及跟@sama Altman的爱恨情仇，
在福布斯最新访谈里Elon聊到 OpenAI 诉讼案时，没有纠结个人恩怨，而是把整个硅谷最不敢摊开讲的一张底牌直接掀开了，
老马说：OpenAI 从非营利强行转为全面营利，正在开创一个极其危险的先例。
很多人看这场官司，以为只是创始人之间的利益撕扯，或者是马斯克因为错过千亿估值而产生的酸葡萄心理。

但马斯克在 2 分多钟里点破的核心，其实是一场动摇整个现代商业慈善根基的特洛伊木马：
如果一家由全免税、免监管的慈善捐赠催化出来、今天估值逼近 8000 亿美元的超级巨头，可以把公益外衣随手脱掉直接装进私人腰包，那么全美甚至全球现有的慈善捐赠契约，就全部从根子上死掉了。

当年 OpenAI 成立时拉着所有人入局的承诺，是一份极度崇高的使命书：
我们是非营利组织，我们为了全人类的利益研发 AGI，防止超级技术被谷歌等商业寡头私有化。

马斯克和其他捐赠人真金白银掏了几千万美元的无偿捐赠，图的不是股权分红，而是公共利益的底线。

后来为了融资买算力，Sam Altman 搞出了一个上限利润的折中结构。

当时各方妥协的关键条款写得清清楚楚：营利实体只负责赚钱还债，一旦真正的通用人工智能（AGI）实现，所有的股权和控制权必须毫无保留地退还给非营利慈善机构。

而最近所有人看到的事实是：
这个曾经用来安抚监管、安抚捐赠人的归还条款，被他们悄无声息地单方面删掉了。

以前慈善信托和免税基金之所以能存在上百年，是因为社会达成了共识：你用免税换取公益，你的成果就永远属于公众。

现在 OpenAI 示范了一条全新的暴富流水线：
先用拯救人类的非营利口号吃尽免税红利、吸纳顶级科学家的奉献和社会的无偿捐款，
等技术突破、商业壁垒铸成之后，反手修改章程，把原本属于公共财产的无价资产，合规洗成几个管理层和华尔街资本瓜分的私产。

如果这一单最终能全身而退，以后世界上就再也没有真正意义上的慈善投资了。

所有的科技巨头都会学着用非营利的幌子孵化核心资产，把研发风险留给纳税人和捐助者，把终局红利留给私人股东，

所以，这早就不是马斯克和 Sam Altman 两个人的战争了，
更像是一场关于公众信任、契约精神与硅谷资本贪婪底线的终极对决。

Tony and I have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.

Customers have 21 meals a week to figure out. Groceries and restaurant delivery each solve part of that problem. Serving customers well means bringing together the best of both.

As the biggest companies in the world move deeper into this market, retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete. They shouldn’t have to become technology companies themselves to stand a chance. Bringing Instacart and DoorDash together can give them a stronger partner in that fight.

For shoppers and Dashers, the opportunity is equally straightforward: less time waiting between orders, more time earning.

I’m incredibly proud of what we built at Instacart and grateful to everyone who helped make it possible. Tony is an extraordinary entrepreneur and leader. I’m excited for Instacart to be part of a founder-led company again, and I can’t wait to see what these two teams build together.

text:
It's been a long time coming... But it's finally time

Part of evolving as a business is recognising where your focus should be while remembering who your users are. 

The reality is that we spent an incredible amount of time purpose-building a network that is specifically designed to cater to HFT and everything that it encompasses. 

Execution needed to be faster and limitations to throughput hindered our ability to run real time risk checks as we think about scaling to 100,000 to 1,000,000 users and beyond. 

For those who have been following along, its no secret that there has been friction between how we execute and what the preference is from Solana leadership. 

I understand and respect their stance, however to continue to frame BULK a solana dex would be reductive to the actual offering, so we’re officially putting this on the record. 

The stronger case is that multichain access expands BULK’s distribution and usable capital while bringing more activity into the same market.

Distribution follows where users hold their money.

As more people enter crypto through neobanks, wallets and payment applications, their first chain may simply be whichever network their provider uses. Their choice of trading venue will depend on execution quality, liquidity and convenience.

Requiring those users to move to a particular chain before they can trade creates an acquisition barrier: another transaction, another fee, another interface and another opportunity to abandon onboarding. It also asks wallets and neobanks to move customers away from their existing infrastructure to integrate BULK.

Multichain access lets BULK meet that distribution where it already exists. A wallet or neobank could offer its customers BULK markets through the rails they already use.

The lesson from multicurrency products like Wise is that a single financial relationship can span across several underlying currencies and payment systems. We expect users to increasingly demand the same convenience across chains.

A unified clearing layer can make capital more productive and markets more liquid.

The strongest clearinghouse analogy is capital efficiency. Traditional clearing infrastructure brings eligible collateral and positions into a common risk framework, allowing qualifying exposures to offset and reducing the capital required to support them. 

This today belongs to CME Group.

For BULK, the opportunity is to connect capital held across supported chains to a common margin system and shared order book. A trader’s access to liquidity should not depend on which chain funded their account. A market maker should be able to serve that combined demand through the same BULK markets.

This creates an economic advantage: more sources of capital and order flow can support deeper books; deeper books can improve execution; better execution can attract more traders and integrations.

That advantage depends on keeping liquidity concentrated. Multichain access should bring users into the same markets, with eligible collateral recognized under a consistent risk framework. It should also let users withdraw available capital through supported destination chains, making BULK useful within their wider financial activity.

BULK’s specialised execution layer gives it a natural role connecting these rails.

BULK is a purpose-built trading L1 rolled into an order book, matching engine and risk engine. Its value comes from how efficiently it executes trades and manages risk. That specialization gives it a reason to serve capital from multiple ecosystems.

Today, collateral lives on Solana, and BULK’s ledger tracks the corresponding balances, positions and margin. Extending that model to supported networks such as Arc, Tempo, Arbitrum and HyperEVM would allow more funding and withdrawal routes to connect to the same execution system.

The architectural principle is to handle each chain’s confirmation and settlement requirements at the funding boundary. Once collateral is securely recognised, trading should run through BULK’s own execution and risk process. This allows BULK to preserve its performance while broadening access.

The intended experience is straightforward: fund from a supported chain, trade against BULK’s shared liquidity, and withdraw available balances to a supported destination. A user could enter from Solana and exit on HyperEVM, with BULK coordinating the accounting, settlement and destination liquidity required.

For wallets and neobanks, that would make BULK an exchange and clearing integration they can use across their supported networks. Each additional rail would expand access to the same venue, and strengthen the market already serving everyone else.

text:
Tony and I have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.

Customers have 21 meals a week to figure out. Groceries and restaurant delivery each solve part of that problem. Serving customers well means bringing together the best of both.

As the biggest companies in the world move deeper into this market, retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete. They shouldn’t have to become technology companies themselves to stand a chance. Bringing Instacart and DoorDash together can give them a stronger partner in that fight.

For shoppers and Dashers, the opportunity is equally straightforward: less time waiting between orders, more time earning.

I’m incredibly proud of what we built at Instacart and grateful to everyone who helped make it possible. Tony is an extraordinary entrepreneur and leader. I’m excited for Instacart to be part of a founder-led company again, and I can’t wait to see what these two teams build together.

@t_xu @DoorDash @Instacart

text:
some lore, since this is one of the trades that changed the direction of my life financially 

late 2020 i had a “good” job, my wife worked, we had a two year old. i'd been learning ta and trading on the side for a couple years, still not confident, mostly following people smarter than me and doing my own work after

i was reading wall street bets at the time. that’s a joke now but in 2020 wsb actually had writeups from people who did real work. you had to dig through the gamblers but there was signal. that's where i found gamestop $gme. there were maybe two or three thesis posts on it total. the roaring kitty guy and one or two others. nobody was in it yet. 

did some research over a few hours and then sold a bunch of etfs, some random stock, threw in some savings from sports betting, scraped together about 100k and put it in immediately (same day) 

that was a lot of money to me then and still is. i put every dollar of it in one shot at a $13 average, pre split. no dca, no tranches

within a few days the ryan cohen news hit and price jumped to 16, 17. from there it was basically a straight line up

i've had some well timed trades in my life and that one is right up there, and it had nothing to do with me being good at ta. it was chance. i happened to read the right post at the right moment. 

what was actually mine was the risk tolerance. i had zero fear and a let's go fucking get this attitude, and that's what put the whole 100k in instead of a sensible 10k or a dca strategy. 

a month or two later that position was worth 3-4 million dollars

i had never seen money like that. it was just on a screen and i was still going to work every day. i told my wife we'd made a million dollars on the way up and she asked if i sold. i said no, it's going higher, we're going to retire off this. she told me it doesn't count until you sell

she was right. i didn't listen. then robinhood turned off the buy button, which people forget about now, and the rally was over right there. 

i ended up selling most of it around a $200 average against a peak near 350. then i got cute and added on the way down and got rinsed on that part too

walked away with low 7 figs after tax. so i left multiple millions on the table and it was still the best trade of my life up to that point. complete life changer i was so happy about. 

and for anyone reading this as a “great trade bro” story, it's not really about that . the trade itself was mostly luck. 

the part i actually controlled was being willing to put on risk that normal people won't put on, so that when the luck showed up i had enough size for it to really change my life. 

you can't control the timing or whether the thesis works but you can control whether you're sized in, and in position if it does

text:
谷歌是我的第一大仓位，从 $260 开始建仓，之后一路加仓，一股没卖。最核心的理由是看好谷歌云。

可持仓这段时间，我一直在骂它的产品。下面几件事，让我真心想问一句：谷歌到底怎么了？

1️⃣ Gemini App 和 Antigravity 的质量，差到不像是谷歌做的。
2️⃣ Gemini 的订阅策略明显失误。同样是捆绑销售，谷歌远不如微软。微软捆的主要是软件，多捆一样成本几乎不涨；谷歌却把 Gemini、云盘、GCP 额度和 YouTube Premium 打包在一起，每一项都有实打实的成本，而且要 GCP 额度的开发者和要 YouTube Premium 的普通用户，根本不是同一群人。
3️⃣ 很多产品都像玩具，比如 GoogleBook、Flow、Gemini Notebook、Stitch。它们真能发展壮大吗？到最后，又有多少会被砍掉？

说到底，谷歌已经很久没有发布过又酷、质量又高的产品了。

马斯克说过，应该买那些你相信产品会越来越好的公司。对照这句话，我一边骂着谷歌的产品，一边冲着谷歌云的增长重仓了它。这是我押得最重的一笔，却不是想得最清楚的一笔。

另外，我买谷歌还有一个原因：Demis。我相信他的愿景。长期来看，我仍然认为谷歌值得持有。

但眼下，这家公司一定在某些地方出了问题。黄仁勋也说过，谷歌技术很强，商业化却做得很差。这是谷歌一贯的老毛病，不意外；可 Gemini App 做得这么差，实在不应该。

Gemini App 不是又一个实验品，它是 AI 时代的入口。把算力让给谷歌云，短期很划算；可如果因此丢掉了这个入口，这笔账最后可能得由搜索来买单。

现在即使 Carbon 重回前沿了，也让人兴奋不起来，因为 Gemini App 和 Antigravity 很烂。

站在用户视角看产品，再考虑投资价值肯定是不全面的，不过吐槽也是真实的，在 Gemini App 没变好之前，我不会再加仓谷歌了。
author: xlcomplete
quoted_text:
我曾经非常看好谷歌的大模型和谷歌云。

理由很简单：Transformer 出自谷歌，这一轮大模型浪潮本来就是它开的头。它有最顶尖的人才，有自研 TPU，论算力储备，没人比它更厚。

但几年过去，事实是 Gemini 一直跟在 Claude 和 GPT 后面。

我现在的看法是：Gemini 落后不是因为能力不够，而是谷歌自己的激励就不往这边推。

1️⃣ 算力是硬约束
需求远大于供给，每一张 TPU 都要做选择：给 Gemini 消费端用，还是放到谷歌云上卖钱？谷歌一直优先保谷歌云。Gemini 消费端的额度、速度、稳定性长期被压着，想追上来只会更难。

2️⃣ 利益分配决定了怎么选
谷歌是 Anthropic 的大股东，而 A社又是谷歌云 TPU 的大客户。算力卖给 A社，谷歌云收入涨，A社估值涨，谷歌手里的股权也跟着涨，一鱼三吃。算力留给 Gemini，就是自己烧钱，再去跟自己投的公司正面竞争。

站在资本的角度，算力先给谷歌云而不是 Gemini，是完全理性的决策。

所以 Gemini 今天的处境不是意外，而是谷歌自己的利益结构推出来的。只要这个结构不变，Gemini 恐怕永远追不上 Anthropic 和 OpenAI。

text:
Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and trade[XYZ] have announced their plan to use Hyperliquid as the infrastructure layer to deploy perpetual futures markets for US traders across crypto, equities, commodities, foreign exchange, and other real-world assets, subject to regulatory approvals. ICE operates NYSE and some of the largest exchanges and clearing houses globally. 

In this structure:
+ Hyperliquid serves as the underlying technology infrastructure via HIP-3*
+ trade[XYZ] designs and implements the markets
+ ICE operates the regulated market and clearing structure

Existing trade[XYZ] HIP-3 markets will remain unchanged.

Hyperliquid is a neutral infrastructure layer with the goal of supporting large parts of the financial system. As with HIP-3, HIP-3* deployers are independent operators who use Hyperliquid as the onchain infrastructure layer for their own markets, while retaining control and responsibility over their deployment.
author: HyperliquidX
quoted_text:
trade[XYZ] and ICE, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, are joining forces to bring 24/7 perpetual futures on Hyperliquid to the United States.

In just over a year, our markets on Hyperliquid have surpassed $650 billion in volume. They provide continuous price discovery for stocks, indices, and commodities, and have become trusted reference points for retail and institutions alike when traditional markets are closed. Much of the world trades them. Until now, Americans could only watch.

We intend to change that. Subject to CFTC approval, trade[XYZ] and ICE plan to establish a new, dedicated U.S. market, with novel exchange and clearing infrastructure built on Hyperliquid. Planned contracts span equities, indices, commodities, FX, and crypto, with access through participating brokers and platforms. We’ll share more on products, eligibility, and timing as approvals progress.

ICE brings more than 25 years of experience operating regulated markets, clearing, and managing risk. trade[XYZ] brings the product development, market design, and technology behind the most liquid and robust markets on Hyperliquid. 

Innovation and the protections of U.S. regulation shouldn’t be a trade-off. Together, we plan to prove it.

ICE is making a strategic investment in trade[XYZ] and joins us in building towards the future of Hyperliquid. A small group of market luminaries is joining as well, beginning with Stan Druckenmiller. For more than four decades, few investors have anticipated the great turns in markets as often as Stan. We’re proud to have him with us for the next one.

We’re building the U.S. market in parallel with our existing HIP-3 markets, which we’ll continue to expand and innovate on. We expect both to flourish. They each have a long road map ahead, from new asset classes to new ways to trade them.

To the Hyperliquid community, whether you were here before us or came because of us, thank you. You took a chance on new markets and you made them matter. You’ll forever be a part of this story.

Anything. Anytime. On ICE[XYZ].

虽然官方并未确认 ICE 就是这笔 OTC 的买方，但这条线索提供了一个高度合理的商业推演：

在战略投资之外，传统资本极有可能已通过 OTC 渠道获取了底层代币，提前完成了“股权+筹码”的双重资产绑定。

至于 hyperliquid:native 那当然是应声上涨，除了 DEX 之外，传统老钱与加密交汇点的叙事越来越明晰了。

text:
A lot of people ask me how the GPU neocloud business works. So I thought I would provide a little bit of an example. This is how GPUs actually get paid for in this market using IREN's public numbers as a reference.

Step 1: the customer signs a multi-year take-or-pay contract and prepays. On IREN's recent 3-year contracts, prepayments covered 45% to 55% of the GPU cost.

Step 2: a lender funds most of the rest, secured by the contracted GPUs. For the Microsoft contract that was investment-grade financing at around 6%, which together with prepayments covers 96% of the GPU capex. For a customer without an investment-grade rating, it was 9% fixed.

Step 3: the data centre is a separate, long-life asset. IREN says it has funded construction with cash so far.

Recent 3-year contracts bring in more than $20M of revenue per MW and pay back the GPUs in around two years. At that payback, 9% instead of 6% on the loan barely changes the economics.

So the customer's prepayment and credit do most of the heavy lifting. Who the customer is matters far more than what the market thinks of AI on any given day, and I think that's the thing to follow.

quoted_text:
Growing up in the United States, NYSE was synonymous with the story of American capitalism. I vividly remember learning about the Buttonwood agreement in 9th grade history class. 24 stockbrokers met under a tree on Wall Street and formed the beginning of what would become the world's financial center. From pits to computers to now onchain markets, America has always led the way in innovating markets to improve price discovery and capital formation. Today the next chapter begins with ICE, trade[XYZ], and Hyperliquid.

ICE started as an electricity-trading platform in 2000, growing to acquire NYSE itself in only 13 years. It is a key infrastructure provider of America’s energy, bond, and mortgage markets. ICE is a rare story of exponential growth of a financial giant over decades, continually embracing innovation and technology.

trade[XYZ] was the first HIP-3 deployer and responsible for spearheading the flourishing global RWA perpetual market today. Only a year ago, trade[XYZ] launched its first RWA perpetual markets. They took a bet on HIP-3, which had just launched after months of tireless development. Having followed their journey from day 1, I cannot overstate how much Shoku and the team have poured into growing these markets to a genuine source of price discovery for the most important assets in the world.

Over the past three years, Hyperliquid has pioneered onchain infrastructure to house all of finance. Hyperliquid is nothing without its world-class builders. I am honored that trade[XYZ] and ICE have chosen to build on Hyperliquid to bring perpetual contracts to America.

When I first spoke to Jeff Sprecher around a year ago, he asked what success looks like to me. I thought for some time and joked that it would be seeing ICE building on Hyperliquid's technology. I could never have predicted the progress that we've made as a community in a single year to make this come true. Excited to see what we can build together next.

百强从来不是终点，而是新的起点。
榜单记录的只是这一刻，真正可贵的，是日复一日的坚持与建设。
无论是在交易、创作还是影响力领域，每一位参与者都在用自己的方式，为这个行业添砖加瓦。

站在台下，我只是众多观众中的一员。看着大家在台上熠熠生辉，心中满是感动和欢喜，一定热泪盈眶。

text:
The way things are moving, I'm starting to believe this won't just be an OKX season.

We might actually be witnessing the beginning of an OKX era.

ICE, the parent company of the NYSE, invested in OKX earlier this year.

Then came OKXICE, with plans to bring tokenized US equities into 24/7 markets.

Some of the biggest companies, including Google, Microsoft and Apple, objected to the proposal.

And ironically, Google is getting absolutely nuked today, down double digits after earnings. Obviously not because of OKX, but the timing is fucking hilarious.

Now look at what happened today.

ICE is partnering with Trade[XYZ] to bring Hyperliquid based perpetual markets into the regulated US financial system.

Over $650 BILLION in trading volume already processed by Trade[XYZ] on Hyperliquid.

And legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller is reportedly backing the initiative.

ICE itself says these products are expected to be distributed through its OKX joint venture, subject to regulatory approval.

Connect the dots.

ICE brings traditional financial infrastructure and regulatory expertise.

Trade[XYZ] brings the products.

Hyperliquid brings the technology.

OKX brings access to a massive global retail audience.

This is much bigger than another exchange fighting for crypto trading volume.

We're talking about a potential future where stocks, commodities, indices, FX and crypto can all be traded around the clock.

Of course, regulatory approvals and actual execution still matter. Nothing is guaranteed.

But I've been in this industry long enough to recognize when a company is positioning itself for something much bigger than the current market cycle.

Other exchanges are fighting for market share.

OKX is positioning itself for a much bigger market.

Seasons come and go. Eras are built.

author: VentureCoinist
quoted_text:
trade[XYZ] and ICE, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, are joining forces to bring 24/7 perpetual futures on Hyperliquid to the United States.

In just over a year, our markets on Hyperliquid have surpassed $650 billion in volume. They provide continuous price discovery for stocks, indices, and commodities, and have become trusted reference points for retail and institutions alike when traditional markets are closed. Much of the world trades them. Until now, Americans could only watch.

We intend to change that. Subject to CFTC approval, trade[XYZ] and ICE plan to establish a new, dedicated U.S. market, with novel exchange and clearing infrastructure built on Hyperliquid. Planned contracts span equities, indices, commodities, FX, and crypto, with access through participating brokers and platforms. We’ll share more on products, eligibility, and timing as approvals progress.

ICE brings more than 25 years of experience operating regulated markets, clearing, and managing risk. trade[XYZ] brings the product development, market design, and technology behind the most liquid and robust markets on Hyperliquid. 

Innovation and the protections of U.S. regulation shouldn’t be a trade-off. Together, we plan to prove it.

ICE is making a strategic investment in trade[XYZ] and joins us in building towards the future of Hyperliquid. A small group of market luminaries is joining as well, beginning with Stan Druckenmiller. For more than four decades, few investors have anticipated the great turns in markets as often as Stan. We’re proud to have him with us for the next one.

We’re building the U.S. market in parallel with our existing HIP-3 markets, which we’ll continue to expand and innovate on. We expect both to flourish. They each have a long road map ahead, from new asset classes to new ways to trade them.

To the Hyperliquid community, whether you were here before us or came because of us, thank you. You took a chance on new markets and you made them matter. You’ll forever be a part of this story.

Anything. Anytime. On ICE[XYZ].

text:
Hyperliquid 系永续要上岸美国，分发给到 ICE-OKX！

来拆分一下合规、产品、分发三层谁在干什么，以及 JV 的审批卡点。

按 ICE 10 月 29 日新闻稿：ICE 与 Trade[XYZ] 达成协议，拟把后者基于 Hyperliquid 部署的永续市场，做成美国受监管结构。

ICE 担任 Trade[XYZ] 受监管市场的独家运营商并对 Trade[XYZ] 做战略投资。

零售侧要另起专用市场与清算安排，刻意和 ICE 现有机构期货、清算业务隔离。

稿面：机构客户不背这套零售交易的对手方风险。

这是「能讲进美国牌照叙事」的前提，不是把离岸 DEX 换张皮。

产品层仍是 Trade[XYZ] + Hyperliquid 栈：短周期、24/7，覆盖 Crypto、股指、商品、外汇等 RWA 类永续。

美国侧还要另起受监管结构，并申请支撑杠杆交易所需的批准。

KYC/AML 过线后，预期通过成为会员的 FCM 触达客户。

分发层则是和 OKX 用户最相关的一截！

稿面写明：零售永续预期经合作方、经纪商、平台分发，其中包括 ICE 与 OKX 的合资。

分工大致是：OKX 出全球零售入口与交易触达，ICE 出受监管市场与清算骨架，Trade[XYZ] 出零售永续产品经验。

OKX 这边的增量，是「合规产品能不能接到自己的用户池」。

JV 本身还要等 broker-dealer/FCM 等批准，审批清单还蛮多的：新市场与清算结构、杠杆相关批准、ICE-OKX JV 的 FCM/BD。

而且离岸 Hyperliquid/Trade[XYZ] 流动性，和未来美国 KYC/AML 永续，是两条路径。

后者主要在合规与可触达人群，但不等于费率更低或深度更好。

若真经 JV 上架，实用问题是：账户和地区怎么切、保证金是否走 FCM 通道、和现有 OKX 合约账户是否隔离。

继续等风来！

以上仅为信息分享，不构成任何投资建议。

text:
Sat down with the Head Chef and Owner of Angie's pizza, Angelo Emiliani, to have some high end Italian food and enjoy the vibe while talking shop about the industry and his take on Italian cuisine.

For context, Angie's Pizza is on the Michelin Star list for Texas.

10/10 imo.

And here's the vibe of the spot: it's all reservation, upscale Italian with good food, good drinks, good atmosphere, nestled in the Houston Heights, a side of town known for quality.

And the moment you walk in, you're feeling that energy of the space, and it just feels right; really makes you feel welcome. It has a super open, but modern feel, and it really makes you wanna sit down for a pizza, especially when you see the traditional pizza oven out in the open like that. And lemme tell you, the fresh made pizzas are amazing. I'd know, I had a classic Margherita and it was fantastic.

But that's not all, Chef Angelo came up to me (I sat down on the bar end) and he walked me through the menu and pointed out the vegetarian options. One thing I should note is this place caters to both audiences. About the only thing they don't do is vegan or gluten free, since bread is the lifeblood of an Italian Pizza and Pasta restaurant, and I can't begin to say more about the pizza and pasta.

For instance, I ordered the tortelloni, and no joke, the filling melts in your mouth with flavor that's out of this world, along with the very simple, but incredible curry-seasoned oil sauce chef Angelo decided to go with. The execution? Flawless. And the best part is how clean it was to eat. When you're dealing with Italian food, keeping that clean but delicious variable in the cooking is key, and chef Angelo has nailed that with every single dish I had there, and this was a full stack of cheese, oil, the works.

I think that's a really important aspect to note, because you can go to a place, have some food and it might be cloying or too much in another way or give you heartburn or a bit of upset, but here I am, sitting down and eating this and enjoying it and the first thing I notice is that word "clean" come to mind.

In cooking, especially Italian, it truly is an art form when you can lock that in, and it accelerates the dish from good Italian to great Italian, well before the master strokes are even made. And I assure you, his menu had some serious master strokes, but I'll save that for you to check out when you get your reservation. You'll want one, trust me.

So as the night went on, Chef Angelo and I sat down together at the bar upstairs, to talk shop about his vision of the restaurant, his dedication to quality, while also keeping that warm, welcoming environment you want from, for instance, a family restaurant. He told me about his tradition to family and his art as an Italian Chef and about how he's dedicated his life to the craft of Italian fine dining, over a few drinks with his lovely wife, Zoey.

And I've gotta say... His staff? Genuine, decent people who run like clockwork. These people are industry professionals at their finest and each is obviously highly skilled and experienced in the world of dining and customer service. No joke, I looked away for a second and I was greeted by a gentleman asking if I'd like a refill; the service is exceptional.

All-in-all, it was a fantastic night, I really learned a lot from Chef Angelo and his staff, about an Italian fine dining establishment that keeps the family feel while keeping the Michelin quality, and I'll definitely be back for another round... Or several.

Angie's Pizza in the heights is a destination, and it's selling something beautiful. I guarantee it.

text:
WHY MORE AI AGENTS DON'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN MORE OUTPUT

I run an autonomous engineering system. For five days it reported 25 worker minutes per accepted result as if that were the cost. It is only a lower bound. Inside the intervals where worker time was actually observed the figure is 167, and the reason is a measurement design most agent setups share.

There is a number almost everyone running AI agents quotes, and almost nobody can defend: how much work the agents are doing.

Not how many are running. Not how many tasks they closed. How much work came out the other end, got reviewed by something that was allowed to say no, and was kept.

I have been running an autonomous engineering system on my own machine for about seven weeks. It dispatches bounded coding tasks to isolated workers, each in its own git worktree, each returning an evidence receipt that an independent reviewer either accepts or blocks. The system records its own cost per accepted result on a dashboard I read every morning. For five days that dashboard said 25 worker minutes per accepted result.

When I went back through the raw data, 85 percent of those accepted results had landed in intervals where the instrument recorded no worker time at all. Restricted to the intervals where worker time was observed, the figure is 167 minutes. The two numbers are 6.6 times apart, and the reported one is the flattering one. The true system-wide cost sits somewhere at or above 25.2 and I cannot tell you where, which is the actual problem: a gauge I steered by every morning was reporting a lower bound as if it were a measurement.

The cause is not exotic. It is polling a worker count on a timer and reconstructing worker time from it. If you are running agents and watching a dashboard, there is a good chance it is built the same way, because that is the easy way to build one.

This article is the whole thing: what I measured, how, what the numbers actually support, what they do not, and a free scorecard that computes the same figures for your own setup, including the check that catches the bug.

What you will get out of it

- A definition of throughput for agent work that survives contact with a reviewer.
- The specific measurement failure that makes agent dashboards flattering, and the check that detects it.
- Real numbers from a real system, with the uncertainty stated instead of hidden.
- A decision procedure for whether to add another worker.
- A working scorecard you can run on your own data.

Chapter 0. The number everybody gets wrong

Three different things get called throughput, and they are not the same thing.

Activity is how many workers are running. It is the easiest to measure and the least useful. A worker that is running is spending money.

Completion is how many tasks reported done. Better, and still not it. An agent reporting success is a hypothesis, not a result. In my own system the self-reported success rate and the reviewed acceptance rate are different numbers, and the gap is the whole point of having a reviewer.

Accepted output is how many tasks an independent reviewer accepted. That is the only one worth optimising, because it is the only one that corresponds to something you can keep.

So the unit is: one accepted result. And the cost of it is worker time, model spend, and the human review time that came with it.

The denominator matters just as much as the numerator, and this is where it falls apart. To say "25 worker minutes per accepted result" you need two measurements from the same window: the worker time spent, and the accepted results produced. If those two are measured by different mechanisms, nothing guarantees they cover the same work. Mine did not, and I did not notice for five days.

Chapter 1. Why more workers can make you slower

Before the measurement problem, the thing being measured.

Adding a worker to an agent system is not like adding a core to a CPU. Every extra worker adds load to shared stages that do not scale with it:

Context acquisition. Each worker has to learn the part of the codebase it is about to touch. That cost is paid per worker, not once. Two workers on adjacent files pay it twice and often learn contradictory things.

Collision and ownership. Two workers that touch the same file produce a merge problem that did not exist before. The fix is one writer per surface, which means that past a certain point extra workers have nothing uncontested left to do.

Review. This is the one that bites. Review capacity is close to fixed, because a reviewer that scales with the workers is just more unreviewed work wearing a hat. Eight workers feeding one review stage do not produce eight times the accepted output. They produce a queue.

Integration. Accepted work still has to land. Branches diverge while they wait. The longer the queue, the more likely a branch needs rework before it can merge, which sends it back to a worker and starts the cycle again.

Abandonment. Work that is never reviewed, never merged, or superseded before it lands is pure cost. In my own repository there are branches sitting at double digit dirty-file counts that will never be merged. Every minute in them was paid for.

The shape of this is a queueing system with a narrow stage in the middle, and the classic property of such systems is that the bottleneck does not move when you add capacity upstream. It gets worse, because the queue in front of it lengthens.

That is a well understood argument and I am not claiming to have discovered it. What I can add is a measurement, and an account of how hard it is to measure honestly.

Chapter 2. Inside the system, in public-safe terms

Enough of the architecture to make the numbers meaningful.

A scheduler fires on a timer. On each tick it reads the current state, decides how many bounded tasks to dispatch, and launches each one as an isolated worker with its own git worktree and its own acceptance contract. A task has a budget and a stop rule written into its brief. When a worker finishes, it writes an evidence receipt: what it changed, what tests it ran, what the output was.

A separate reviewer reads the receipt and the diff and writes a verdict file. The verdict is ACCEPTED or it is not, and a non-acceptance has to carry a demonstrated failure, not an opinion. That rule exists because reviewers that block on taste produce infinite loops.

Accepted work merges. The verdict files stay on disk as the permanent record. That record is the dataset in this article: a directory of verdict files with timestamps, and a scheduler log with one line per tick.

Two numbers from the scheduler log matter for what follows, and both are printed on every single line of it:

- The worker count at that moment.
- The task timeout: 1100 seconds, which is 18.3 minutes. No worker can live longer than that.

Chapter 3. The measurement, and the bug inside it

The window: 2026-10-17 07:47 to 2026-10-22 04:48, local time. 342 scheduler ticks. 89 verdict files written inside the window: 66 accepted, 23 not accepted. Acceptance rate 0.74.

Worker time is not logged directly. It is reconstructed, which is where the trouble starts. Each tick records the worker count at that instant. The estimate treats that count as constant until the next tick, multiplies by the gap, and sums. Over the window that gives 1,666 worker minutes. Divide by 66 accepted results and you get 25.2 worker minutes per accepted result. That is the number the dashboard reported, and the number I believed.

Now the part I missed. The scheduler ticks every 20 minutes. I checked the gaps between all 342 ticks: the median is 20.0 minutes, the shortest is 16.7. And the maximum worker lifetime, printed on every line of the same log, is 18.3 minutes.

The sampler is slower than the thing it is sampling.

A worker that starts after one tick and finishes before the next is never seen. The interval is recorded as zero workers, and every minute that worker spent is counted as zero. Recorded as zero and did not run look identical in the data.

Be careful about how strong a claim that is. 18.3 minutes is the maximum worker lifetime, not the minimum, so a 20 minute interval makes a complete miss possible; it does not prove that every short worker was missed, and some workers clearly were seen. The reverse is also worth stating plainly, because it is the trap I nearly wrote into this article: no fixed polling interval guarantees you see everything. Halving the interval to 9.2 minutes would bound misses for workers that last longer than the interval and would do nothing at all for a worker that lives 90 seconds. Polling faster narrows the hole. Only per-worker start and end events close it.

So I went back and asked a question I should have asked first: for each accepted result, what was the recorded worker count in the interval it landed in?

Concurrent workers recorded / Wall hours / Worker minutes / Accepted / Not accepted / Worker min per accepted
|---|---|---|---|---|---
0 / 89.5 / 0 / 56 / 19 / undefined
1 / 20.2 / 1,212 / 9 / 4 / 134.7
2 / 3.3 / 393 / 1 / 0 / 392.7
3 / 0.3 / 61 / 0 / 0 / undefined
All / 113.3 / 1,666 / 66 / 23 / 25.2

Fifty six of the sixty six accepted results, 85 percent of them, landed in intervals where the instrument recorded zero workers. Those results have no measured cost at all. They were divided into a pile of worker minutes they had nothing to do with.

All 1,666 measured worker minutes sit in the non-zero rows by definition, and those rows contain 10 accepted results. Restricted to the intervals where worker time was observed, the figure is 1,666 divided by 10, or 166.6 worker minutes per accepted result. The two numbers are 6.6 times apart.

Be precise about what each of those numbers is, because this is exactly where it is easy to cheat.

25.2 is a lower bound, not an estimate. Every accepted result is counted in the denominator, but the numerator is an undercount of worker time, since unobserved workers contribute zero. True worker minutes are at least 1,666, so the true cost per accepted result is at least 25.2 and could be anything above it.

166.6 is a conditional figure, not the true cost. It is the cost per accepted result within the intervals where worker time was observed, and those intervals were selected by the instrument rather than at random. It rests on 10 accepted results.

The true system-wide figure is unknown. Attribution coverage of 0.152 is not a correction factor; it is a statement that 85 percent of the output cannot be tied to any measured cost. No arithmetic on this dataset recovers the real number. What the dataset does support, firmly, is that the reported figure was a floor presented as a measurement, and the gap between it and the attributable figure is a factor of 6.6.

Why so many zero-worker intervals? Two reasons, and I can only partly separate them. Some is the aliasing above: short workers born and dead inside one 20 minute gap. Some is lag: a verdict file is written when the review is written, which can be well after the work. Both push accepted results into intervals where no worker time was recorded, and both are properties of the instrument rather than the system being measured. That is the uncomfortable part. The instrument was wrong in a way that made the system look better.

What about 1 worker versus 2?

The table hints at the thing the article is named after: 134.7 worker minutes per accepted at one worker, 392.7 at two. Nearly three times worse.

I am not going to tell you that is a result. It rests on 9 accepted results in one bucket and 1 in the other. The worker count was chosen by a governor reacting to machine load, so the two-worker periods are the busier, more contended periods by construction. Task difficulty was not held constant. Any of those could produce this on its own.

What it is: a directionally consistent observation, too small to carry weight, in a system where the mechanism that would cause it is already known to exist. The right response is not to publish it as a finding. It is to run the controlled version, which I will, and which the scorecard below is built to record.

If you came here for "15 agents are slower than 3, here is the graph", I do not have that graph and neither does anyone else I have been able to find. What I have is the measurement framework, one real dataset with its flaws exposed, and the specific instrument bug that makes most such graphs untrustworthy.

Chapter 4. Where the bottleneck actually sits

Strip the measurement problem away and look at the shape of the window.

113.3 wall hours. Workers recorded as running for 20.2 hours of it at one worker, 3.3 at two, 0.3 at three. For roughly 79 percent of the wall clock the system recorded no workers at all, and yet most of the accepted work shows up in those stretches.

Even allowing generously for unobserved workers, the picture is of a system that is not worker-bound. It is bound by what happens between dispatches: deciding what to dispatch, reviewing what came back, and merging it. Adding workers to that system buys very little, and the thing it does buy most reliably is a longer review queue.

This is the practical reason the "add more agents" instinct disappoints. High worker utilisation is not a goal. It is only good if accepted output per worker hour holds up as you add them. When the constrained stage is review or integration, the sign of improvement is not busier workers. It is the queue in front of review getting shorter.

Chapter 5. The governor, as a design pattern

If a worker is not the unit of capacity, something has to decide when work is dispatched at all. In my system that is a governor, and I am describing it here as a pattern rather than claiming a verified product.

The governor holds a small number of rules:

- Objective fidelity. A task that does not serve the current objective does not get dispatched, however good it looks. Found-it-so-build-it is how a week disappears.
- Previously accepted evidence. If a question was already answered and the answer was accepted, it is not re-opened without a demonstrated reason.
- Bounded exploration. Every task has a budget and a stop rule. Over budget is a blocked result, not a slow green one.
- Action risk classes. Reversible and in scope runs without asking. Spending money, sending something outward, or anything irreversible stops and asks a human.
- Stop and escalate. Conflict between owners, a failed safety floor, or a missing permission stops mutation and preserves state.

The honest status line: these are implemented and in use. They are not independently verified as a product, and this article is not a release announcement for them. The reason they are relevant here is that every one of them reduces the number of workers you need, which is a cheaper lever than adding workers.

Chapter 6. The scorecard you can use

The companion artifact is a single page with no dependencies, no network calls, no analytics and no storage. You can download two files and open it from your filesystem. Nothing you type leaves the page.

It does three jobs.

One: it checks your instrument before it computes anything. Enter your sampler period and the shortest worker lifetime you care about observing. It tells you whether a worker can slip between two samples, and it refuses to describe any polling interval as a guarantee. With my real numbers, a 20 minute interval and an 18.3 minute maximum lifetime, it returns:

CAN MISS WORKERS. A worker shorter than the 20 min interval can start and finish unseen. Sampling every 9.2 min would bound misses for workers longer than that interval, and still not for shorter ones. Per-worker start and end events are the only reliable fix.

Two: it scores a measurement window. Attempted, accepted, rejected, wall hours, worker hours, review hours, model cost. It returns acceptance ratio, accepted per worker hour, worker minutes per accepted, cost per accepted, integration ratio and rework share.

It also has a field most dashboards do not: accepted results that fall inside observed worker time. The ratio of that to total accepted is the attribution coverage. At coverage 1 your cost figure is sound. My window scores 0.152, and the tool flags attribution as broken, shows both figures side by side, 25.2 across all accepted results and 166.6 within observed intervals, and labels the first a lower bound rather than a result. It does not pretend the gap is a correction factor. That contrast is the single most useful thing the tool does.

Three: it compares two windows and gives a verdict. Load the measured one-worker and two-worker windows and it returns:

SCALING HURT. Accepted per worker hour 0.446 to 0.153. Change: minus 65.7 percent.

with a line underneath reminding you that a difference between two windows is not a controlled result.

Two deliberate choices in the code. Every ratio with an empty denominator returns null, never zero and never infinity, because a missing measurement and a measured zero are different facts and conflating them is how you end up with a confident wrong number. And a measured zero is a verdict: a window that produced nothing in an observed hour of worker time has told you something real.

The whole calculation core is 145 lines, 94 of them code, with 18 tests covering division by zero, missing fields, negative inputs, accepted exceeding attempted, worker hours exceeding workers times wall hours, unit conversion, the sampling-interval boundary cases and extreme values. The tests run with node --test. One of them caught a real mistake I had made in the comparison logic, where I had treated a measured zero as an absence. That is the same category of error as the one this entire article is about, which I think is the honest note to end the engineering on.

Chapter 7. How to apply this on Monday

In order, because the order matters.

1. Check whether a worker can slip between two of your samples. Compare your polling interval with the shortest worker you care about. If a worker can start and finish inside one interval, your worker time is an undercount and your cost per accepted result is a floor, not a measurement. Polling faster shrinks the hole for longer workers and never closes it for short ones.

2. Define accepted before you measure anything. Something independent of the worker has to be allowed to say no, and a rejection has to carry a demonstrated reason rather than a preference. Without that, throughput is just activity with better branding.

3. Measure worker time, do not reconstruct it. This is the real fix and it is not a faster sampler. Have each worker record its own start and end. Worker hours then become a sum of measured intervals, attribution coverage goes to 1 by construction, and the polling question disappears instead of getting smaller. I am moving to that; a faster tick is only a stopgap that reduces the hole for long workers.

4. Find the constrained stage before adding capacity. If review and integration are waiting on work, more workers help. If work is waiting on review, more workers make it worse. You can usually tell by looking at how long something sits between accepted and merged.

5. Spend on routing before spending on workers. Better task boundaries, one writer per surface, and a clear acceptance contract raise accepted output per worker hour without adding a single worker.

6. Add one worker, then measure the same window again. Not two. If accepted per worker hour falls, you have your answer, and it cost you one experiment.

The limits of all of this

The things I would attack if I were reading this.

- One system, one operator, five days. Not a benchmark. My workloads are not yours.
- The 166.6 figure rests on 10 accepted results, in intervals the instrument selected rather than a random sample. It is a conditional figure, not a replacement true value.
- The true system-wide cost per accepted result is unknown. 25.2 is a lower bound. Nothing in this dataset identifies the real number, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
- The one versus two worker comparison is observational and tiny. Treat it as a hypothesis with a mechanism, nothing more.
- Verdict timestamps lag the work, so some of the zero-worker mass is lag rather than missed workers. This dataset cannot separate the two. Recording work start and end directly fixes both at once, and I have not done it yet.
- The acceptance standard is mine. A stricter reviewer would lower every acceptance ratio here. Throughput measured against a weak reviewer is a vanity number, and no tool can detect that for you.
- No controlled experiment yet. The protocol is: fixed task family, fixed model route, fixed reviewer, randomised worker count, at least 30 accepted results per arm. That is the next issue.

The right question

"How many agents can I run" is a question about your budget. It has an easy, expensive answer.

The question that pays is: what gets accepted, how fast, at what total cost, and with how much of my attention? Every one of those has a denominator, and a denominator you cannot defend is not a measurement.

The reason I am opening with my own broken gauge rather than a clean result is that the broken gauge is the more useful finding. Anyone can produce a chart with agent counts on one axis. Almost nobody shows you whether their instrument could see what it was counting, or whether the number on the dashboard is a measurement or a floor. Mine was a floor for five days while I read it every morning.

Check yours. The scorecard will tell you in about a minute, and if your answer is the same as mine, the fix is to stop polling and start recording.

The scorecard is free and runs entirely in your browser. No signup, no network calls, no analytics, nothing stored.

https://t.co/nsE6rnodLM

The full article, the dataset table and the method also live at https://t.co/Dsy5PkivNx if you would rather read it there.

Next issue: the controlled version of this experiment, with worker timing recorded properly and the protocol fixed in advance.

author: NYSE
quoted_text:
trade[XYZ] and ICE, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, are joining forces to bring 24/7 perpetual futures on Hyperliquid to the United States.

In just over a year, our markets on Hyperliquid have surpassed $650 billion in volume. They provide continuous price discovery for stocks, indices, and commodities, and have become trusted reference points for retail and institutions alike when traditional markets are closed. Much of the world trades them. Until now, Americans could only watch.

We intend to change that. Subject to CFTC approval, trade[XYZ] and ICE plan to establish a new, dedicated U.S. market, with novel exchange and clearing infrastructure built on Hyperliquid. Planned contracts span equities, indices, commodities, FX, and crypto, with access through participating brokers and platforms. We’ll share more on products, eligibility, and timing as approvals progress.

ICE brings more than 25 years of experience operating regulated markets, clearing, and managing risk. trade[XYZ] brings the product development, market design, and technology behind the most liquid and robust markets on Hyperliquid. 

Innovation and the protections of U.S. regulation shouldn’t be a trade-off. Together, we plan to prove it.

ICE is making a strategic investment in trade[XYZ] and joins us in building towards the future of Hyperliquid. A small group of market luminaries is joining as well, beginning with Stan Druckenmiller. For more than four decades, few investors have anticipated the great turns in markets as often as Stan. We’re proud to have him with us for the next one.

We’re building the U.S. market in parallel with our existing HIP-3 markets, which we’ll continue to expand and innovate on. We expect both to flourish. They each have a long road map ahead, from new asset classes to new ways to trade them.

To the Hyperliquid community, whether you were here before us or came because of us, thank you. You took a chance on new markets and you made them matter. You’ll forever be a part of this story.

Anything. Anytime. On ICE[XYZ].

text:
Anthropic has filed for a record $2 trillion IPO. In a talk uploaded November 30, 2025, a stockbroker asked Elon Musk which company he would buy. Musk said he has no portfolio, then named Google and Nvidia.

The man asking is Nikhil Kamath, who told Musk his primary job is stockbroker and stock investor. Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, xAI and X, and says the output of AI and robotics "will dwarf everything else."

The clip is three moments from a 114-minute conversation. The full talk is free on YouTube. In it Musk says US deficits run on the order of $2 trillion a year, and that interest payments on the debt exceed the entire US military budget.

His rules for money fit on a napkin.

Judge the product, not the price. His test for any stock: do you like what the company makes, do you like the roadmap, do you believe in the team. A company, he says, is a group of people assembled to make products and services.

Expect the swings. That test does not solve for daily moves, which he admits are sometimes pretty extreme. His advice is to hold and not worry about them.

Watch the ratio. Inflation, he says, is goods and services output against growth in the money supply. AI has not yet raised output enough. He guesses output growth passes money growth in about three years.

Know the fix on offer. He says the only thing that can solve the US debt is AI and robotics. That is a bet, and he says so.

Money is a tool. He calls it an information system for labor allocation. A trillion dollars on a desert island buys nothing, because there is no labor to allocate.

Check who owns it. When he says AI, robotics and maybe spaceflight will hold almost all the value, he runs companies in each of those fields.

"I don't look for things to invest in. I just try to build things."

Listen from 86:12.

Before you buy into any IPO this month, write down what the company sells, what it ships next and who builds it. If you cannot fill in all three lines, you are not investing. You are buying a headline with your name on it.

text:
卧槽！神预言咯！谷歌搜索的增速从 17% 掉到了 12%。三个月前，就有个每月在谷歌广告上花 50 万美元以上的广告主发帖说，这个增长是“人为做出来的”。

他叫 Max Anderson。他说搜索量在被大模型分流，谷歌靠两个办法撑收入：你出价精确匹配的词，谷歌会拿去匹配一堆不相关的搜索词，照样收钱，还关不掉；每天 1000 美元的预算，会花到 2000 美元以上。

这两个做法都有据可查。2024 年反垄断案的判决里，法官 Mehta 认定广告主关不掉关键词匹配，只能一个个加否定词去挡。日预算一天最多花到 2 倍，是谷歌帮助页上写明的规则，月底总花费不超过日预算乘 30.4 天。判决里还写到，谷歌给广告涨价是一点一点涨，好让广告主把涨价当成拍卖里的正常波动。

但他说的“搜索量在降”，财报对不上。皮查伊说，这个季度搜索查询量的同比增速是五年来最高。

增速为什么掉，Philipp Schindler 在电话会上讲了几条：最大的一项是汇率，其余是欧盟取消小额包裹免税、世界杯广告预算更多落在 6 月；还有一条，AI Mode 的查询涨得很快，但变现比传统搜索低。

数字上，付费点击增速从 13% 掉到 8%，每次点击的均价涨 4%（上一季是 3%）。搜索多出来的收入，大半来自点击数，不是涨价。

Max 说对的是 AI 在拉低搜索的变现，说错的是搜索量在降。下一份财报我只盯一个数：付费点击增速。13%，8%，看下一个是多少。 $GOOGL
author: alanchen
quoted_text:
As someone who has personally spent $500k / mo+ on Google Ads for years, I can tell you with certainty: 

This revenue growth in Search is artificial & extremely unhealthy for Google’s business long term

Search volumes are declining as legacy search is being increasingly cannibalized by non-monetized LLM queries

Google’s response? 

Manufacture revenue growth via short-sighted, highly extractive, customer-hostile tactics. I.e. charge advertisers more for lower quality clicks, including clicks they do not want and explicitly did not approve Google to charge them for

A few examples to illustrate: 

For all of its history until recently, Google operated on a 2nd price auction model

I.e. if you bid $5 CPC and the next highest bidder bids $1 CPC, Google charged you $1.01 for the click (one penny more than the 2nd highest bidder) rather than the $5 you bid

This was a genius move by Google early on as it incentivizes advertisers to input their true maximum willingness to pay rather than trying to play the game of bidding low and constantly adjusting to try to stay just ahead of the next highest bidder while still not paying too much

However recently, Google silently deprecated the 2nd price auction and began charging advertisers as much as their bid and budget caps allow, regardless of what anyone else is bidding

It’s a short-sighted cash grab at the expense of the long term health of the  advertiser ecosystem

Making thing worse, Google also recently nerfed keyword targeting precision

Google previously had precise keyword targeting settings that allowed advertisers pick individual search phrases to bid on, defined down to the character w/ exact match or phrase match targeting 

This was one of the core features that made search advertising magic, enabling advertisers to run extremely precise campaigns based on exactly what their target customer typed 

But now, even if you bid on a specific term or phrase using the strictest exact 
-match targeting settings, Google will show your ad across 1000’s of unrelated keywords, labeling them as as “exact match (close variant)” 

The definition of “close variant” means whatever they want it to and changes constantly. The result is advertisers get billed for clicks that are totally irrelevant to their business and that their targeting settings explicitly forbid Google from targeting. Google does it anyway and there’s no ability to turn this off

So now exact match is broad match, and broad match is just meaningless spam

This is all very bad for advertisers, but for Google, it allows them to show your ad and bill you for clicks across 1000x more searches that were previously going unmonetized (mainly because they’re garbage queries no one wants) 

This is how you grow revenue atop declining search volumes 

Lastly, and perhaps most egregiously, Google quietly stopped respecting budget caps by a factor of 2x. For example campaigns we’ve been running for years with $1000 daily budget caps suddenly began spending $2000+ per day 

And the extra spend is entirely on the garbage keywords Google arbitrarily throws in as “exact match (close variants)” which have no value to our business, but can’t be turned off

Google offers no refunds nor any recourse for overspend or spend on keywords you explicitly did not target

These are not the actions of a healthy business. These are the actions of company whose core business is in decline but desperately needs to pump quarterly earnings so Wall Street will continue to fund insane capex while hopefully looking through their rapidly deteriorating negative free cash flow 

Google operated a benevolent monopoly for the better part of 25 yrs

Meaning the value Google captured from Search was but a small fraction of the value it created, and that spread produced a potential energy that justified expectations of high earnings growth far, far into the future 

This is now no longer the case

At the alter of AI capex, Google is sacrificing the golden goose

text:
现任 Anthropic Claude Code 核心成员、前 Google Chrome 工程总监 Addy Osmani刚发了篇长文，直接点破了很多人现在的 AI 编程误区：你大概率一直在“过度提示”（Overprompting）Claude。

最扎心的一个事实是：Anthropic 官方把 Claude Code 的系统提示词直接砍掉了 80%，结果模型代码跑分一点都没掉！

很多人还在用一两年前伺候老模型的那套“保姆式习惯”写 Prompt，字数越堆越多。面对 Opus 5.5 这代新模型，真正高手都在做减法：

1. 别教它怎么走，只给两件事： 一句话说清「终极目标是什么」+「怎么验证做对了」。只要你给它一个能跑出 Pass/Fail 的单测或判定脚本，它自己就能死磕闭环到底，根本不用你寸步不离地盯着。

2. 别迷信复杂的多 Agent 架构： 很多人喜欢无脑堆 Subagents，但 Addy 直言：子智能体不仅不会让事情变聪明，还会让延迟和账单成倍暴涨。从实测来看，「单个带 Skills 的 Agent」在代码质量和性价比上往往完胜多 Agent 编排。

3. 不知道怎么做，就让它反向面试你： 需求不明确时，别硬憋 Prompt。让 Claude 提问面试你，直到它能整理出一份完整的需求 Spec；然后开个新会话，拿着这份 Spec 丢给它直接开工。

4. 别当人肉代码扫描机： 代码写完，先调一个没看过聊天记录的独立 Agent 去把 Diff 审一遍、改一轮。把低级问题全甩给机器，人类只留着精力给核心业务风险做最终裁判。

一句话总结： 模型每升级一代，你最该做的第一件事不是拼命加规则，而是赶紧去提示词里“删代码”。每隔几个月给你的 Prompt 瘦一次身，别用伺候老模型的旧习惯，束缚了新模型的发挥。

author: matthuang
quoted_text:
trade[XYZ] and ICE, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, are joining forces to bring 24/7 perpetual futures on Hyperliquid to the United States.

In just over a year, our markets on Hyperliquid have surpassed $650 billion in volume. They provide continuous price discovery for stocks, indices, and commodities, and have become trusted reference points for retail and institutions alike when traditional markets are closed. Much of the world trades them. Until now, Americans could only watch.

We intend to change that. Subject to CFTC approval, trade[XYZ] and ICE plan to establish a new, dedicated U.S. market, with novel exchange and clearing infrastructure built on Hyperliquid. Planned contracts span equities, indices, commodities, FX, and crypto, with access through participating brokers and platforms. We’ll share more on products, eligibility, and timing as approvals progress.

ICE brings more than 25 years of experience operating regulated markets, clearing, and managing risk. trade[XYZ] brings the product development, market design, and technology behind the most liquid and robust markets on Hyperliquid. 

Innovation and the protections of U.S. regulation shouldn’t be a trade-off. Together, we plan to prove it.

ICE is making a strategic investment in trade[XYZ] and joins us in building towards the future of Hyperliquid. A small group of market luminaries is joining as well, beginning with Stan Druckenmiller. For more than four decades, few investors have anticipated the great turns in markets as often as Stan. We’re proud to have him with us for the next one.

We’re building the U.S. market in parallel with our existing HIP-3 markets, which we’ll continue to expand and innovate on. We expect both to flourish. They each have a long road map ahead, from new asset classes to new ways to trade them.

To the Hyperliquid community, whether you were here before us or came because of us, thank you. You took a chance on new markets and you made them matter. You’ll forever be a part of this story.

Anything. Anytime. On ICE[XYZ].

text:
Been watching these TikTok LIVE streams lately and something caught my attention.

People are literally spending thousands of dollars gifting random strangers. Some pretty girl talking bullshit, some dude acting like a macho man, two idiots doing PvP battles and their supporters throwing money at each other.

And the funniest part? Nobody is expecting any money back. They spend $1,000, get their name shouted out, win some stupid battle and come back tomorrow to do it again.

Now think about meme coins.

We have millions of degens gambling every day, but the moment someone buys $1,000 worth of a meme and it becomes $800, he's ready to declare the entire industry a scam.

I was thinking, what the fk is TikTok doing right that we're not?

Both are basically running on dopamine. Both have communities, competition, whales, attention seekers and people who want to feel important.

But somehow TikTok has figured out how to make losing money enjoyable, while in crypto even making money isn't enough because everyone wants to make MORE.

I think this is something meme coin platforms and builders seriously need to look into.

We keep building faster chains, cheaper swaps, better launchpads, but we're barely experimenting with the psychology that makes people happily spend money on absolutely nothing.

There is clearly a massive amount of money sitting outside crypto that's already being spent on digital entertainment every single day.

We don't necessarily need to convince those people to become traders. We need to figure out what makes them spend in the first place and build something worth participating in.

TikTok users spend money to win a battle that means nothing. Crypto users won't even hold a winning coin for more than five minutes.

Somewhere in that difference is a fking massive opportunity.

text:
Why am I so interested in $宝拉 (POLAR/PAULA) on X Layer?

I think people are overlooking something interesting here, so let me explain my thesis.

We've spent years in crypto gambling on dogs, frogs, cats and every other animal imaginable.

But outside our little crypto bubble, something much bigger has been happening.

Pop Mart did over $5 BILLION in revenue last year. The Monsters, the IP family behind Labubu, generated roughly $2 BILLION alone.

The company is valued at around $22 BILLION.

Think about that for a second. People are spending billions collecting dolls.

And here we are arguing whether a frog or a dog deserves another billion-dollar market cap.

Now here's where it gets interesting.

On September 24, Pop Mart released its new POLAR Smudge Puff collection.

I started looking deeper into the character.

POLAR isn't some random AI-generated mascot created yesterday to launch a token. It's an actual Pop Mart collectible character with multiple releases dating back to 2024.

And now there's a community meme around it on OKX's X Layer, paired with Pop Mart stock exposure.

Meanwhile, OKX already offers trading exposure to Pop Mart stock, and X Layer has been actively developing its RWA meme ecosystem.

I'm not saying Pop Mart is backing this token. It isn't an equity claim on the company either.

What interests me is the possibility of connecting two completely different cultures.

One where people spend billions collecting physical characters.

Another where people spend billions speculating on digital memes.

And I genuinely think crypto has done a terrible job bringing these two audiences together.

Imagine if even a fraction of the enthusiasm behind collectible culture eventually found its way into on-chain communities.

That's the opportunity I'm interested in.

Of course, a popular character alone doesn't guarantee a successful token. We still need genuine holders, liquidity, community and longevity.

Statement on the $AXIS Sell-off of 28–29 October

Over the past two days, a series of addresses sold a large volume of $AXIS on-chain. We want to set out clearly what these tokens were and what we are doing about it.

1. No team or investor tokens were sold.
All Core Team and investor allocations, together with every other locked allocation, 835,000,000 $AXIS (83.5% of total supply), remain in the vesting contract, which is jointly administered with Binance: 0xAFE41cfd4C21f1D896678e32C5AD456ea41835e6. Anyone can verify the balance on BaseScan. Not a single token has left it, and none unlocks before the 12-month cliff.

2. Where the sold tokens came from.
The tokens sold came from the initial circulating supply set out in our published tokenomics, specifically part of the Ecosystem allocation. Many ecosystem recipients are not crypto-native, so their allocation was delivered through a single OTC counterparty, under a written agreement that includes lock-up terms.

3. What we believe happened.
The pattern of the sales, which went through exchange deposit routes and hundreds of fresh addresses within hours of delivery, strongly suggests that the OTC counterparty sold these tokens on the open market. If so, this is inconsistent with the agreement.

4. What we are doing.
- We have suspended all further dealings with this counterparty.
- We are reviewing the agreement with legal counsel and will pursue every remedy available under it.
- Going forward, any remaining Ecosystem tokens will be distributed only through on-chain vesting.

The team‘s tokens remain locked, and our commitment to building Axis is unchanged.

text:
Some thoughts on market makers, transparency & the @Forgd_ leaderboard:

Yesterday, a ranking of crypto market makers made the rounds on X and generated a lot of debate.

For context, the ranking was copy + pasted directly from a leaderboard built by @Forgd_, hosted on @DefiLlama & @Tokenomist_ai.

Importantly, this leaderboard benchmarks market makers engaged by blockchain projects to support liquidity for their native tokens – not prop trading firms deploying their own balance sheets.

It grades MMs based on a combination of:

→ Historical trade activity
→ KPI adherence
→ Venue coverage & treasury management capabilities
→ Size of client base

It’s also only one of several leaderboards we publish. You can separately see which desks historically provide the deepest liquidity, generate the most maker volume, maintain the tightest spreads, and demonstrate the strongest uptime. https://t.co/ECYXzadMCb

Is the methodology perfect? Absolutely not.

But there are far too many people in crypto claiming to have alpha on “who the best market makers are” based almost entirely on gut instinct and anecdotal evidence.

After spending more than a decade in crypto (including time working at CEXs & market makers myself) I’ve probably been asked “Who are the best MMs?” hundreds of times.

I wanted to take a shot at answering that question with actual data.

So, some context on why we built these tools, how the data works, what the leaderboard does and does NOT tell you, and where I think we can improve 👇

1. Why we built it

One thing worth acknowledging: Forgd wasn’t the first company to recognize this problem.

Before we launched, other firms were already helping projects connect with market makers, structure deals, and better understand how their liquidity providers were performing. I think they deserve credit for helping validate an important thesis: market making was an enormous black box for most token issuers.

Where we wanted to take a different approach was accessibility.

We didn’t think projects should need to pay large advisory fees or recurring SaaS subscriptions simply to understand whether their market maker was doing its job.

So we built self-service tools that projects can use completely free of charge to:

→ Monitor market maker performance
→ Run competitive MM RFQs
→ Compare proposals
→ Benchmark historical MM performance
→ Make more informed decisions

Our belief was pretty simple: GTM infrastructure should be broadly accessible.

Today, hundreds of projects across virtually every sector and stage use Forgd’s infrastructure.

Some projects like @zama, @MeteoraAG and @metaplex have taken that a step further by making their market maker performance & engagement structures publicly transparent through products like “Universal Token Ratings”.

We think that’s a good thing. The more transparency projects are willing to provide around how their market makers trade, where they provide liquidity, and how engagements are structured, the better informed the entire industry becomes.

And because the tools are free, adoption has given us something extremely valuable: sample size.

Since launching in Q4 2024, we’ve tracked nearly 600 market maker engagements across 30+ market makers, creating what we believe is one of the largest structured datasets for understanding how crypto market makers actually perform across real engagements.

2. How does the methodology actually work?

TL;DR: 
i. Projects use Forgd to monitor their market makers. For every integrated engagement, the market maker transmits trading activity to Forgd through a standardized API integration.

ii. Through these integrations, we capture things like maker fill volume, liquidity depth, spreads, KPI adherence and other engagement-specific data on a per-project, per-exchange and per-trading-pair basis.

iii. Separately, Forgd independently consumes market-wide data directly from exchanges and on-chain infrastructure. That means we can observe not only what the market maker says it did, but what was happening across the broader market.

put simply...
→ The API tells us what the market maker did.
→ Our independent market infrastructure tells us what the broader market looked like.

We can then calculate things like the MM’s share of total maker volume or total order book depth and evaluate its activity in the context of the entire market rather than looking at an isolated number.

We aggregate those observations at the project level and then across each market maker’s engagements to understand how that desk performs on average for the projects we monitor.

That allows us to compare things like:

→ Average depth of liquidity
→ Average maker / taker fill volume
→ Average spreads
→ KPI adherence / uptime
→ Engagement structures
→ Average loan sizes
→ Loan + option vs. retainer + working capital usage
→ Other commercial considerations

If you want to nerd out on the actual methodology, including examples of how raw data is transformed into project-level and MM-level observations, we published the full documentation here: https://t.co/AoiqfMFbbd

Some people will like the methodology. Some will hate it. That’s totally fine!

I’d much rather publish the methodology, expose it to criticism, and continuously improve it than pretend we’ve somehow solved market maker benchmarking forever!

3. There are also important limitations.

Our dataset is large, but it is not comprehensive.

Forgd has tracked nearly 600 market maker engagements since launching, but we obviously don’t capture every token project or every market maker in crypto.

Our software is free to use by design. We wanted to democratize access to tools that let projects monitor their market makers, understand how they’re trading, and make better-informed decisions without putting that infrastructure behind a paywall.

That model has given us a very robust sample size, but we can’t force every project to use it.
The same applies to market makers. Desks like @wintermute_t, @CumberlandSays, @jump_ , and @FalconXGlobal aren’t currently included because they aren’t integrated with our platform.

Does that mean they’re bad market makers? Or that they’re “hiding something”?

Absolutely not.

My experiences with these desks throughout my career has been extremely positive, and I think they can be fantastic partners for projects launching tokens.

Integration takes engineering resources, and these firms have their own development priorities. Hopefully we can convince more of them to integrate over time and make the dataset even stronger.

On the flip side, I want to give credit to desks like @flowdesk_co, @GSR_io, @ambergroup_io, @SeliniCapital, @keyrock, @jpegtrading, @tophash and others that have invested time integrating with Forgd and working with our team to improve the infrastructure.

Longer term, I think transparency around token liquidity is only going to become more important.

I’d love to see a world where projects proactively disclose who their market makers are, how those engagements are structured, and (retroactively, T + 1) how those desks actually traded across different venues.

That kind of transparency would give the investing public much better visibility into a token’s market structure, including the ability to distinguish organic liquidity and volume from liquidity and volume being subsidized through formal market maker engagements.

We’re obviously not there yet.

But the more projects & MMs that participate in initiatives like Universal Token Ratings (https://t.co/7iiglMFxyO) & Token Transparency Framework by @Blockworks / @JasonYanowitz, the more complete the picture becomes. Our goal is to build the free infrastructure that makes providing that transparency as easy as possible.

4. A note on competition

I’ve seen plenty of criticism and debate around the methodology. That’s okay. In fact, I think it’s healthy.

We’re always looking for ways to improve the methodology, and thoughtful criticism helps us do that.

More broadly, competition is one of the healthiest forces in any industry. It forces everyone to build better products, serve customers better and continuously raise the standard. Web3 market infrastructure should be no different.

In fact, some of the companies we now compete with helped validate the original problem we set out to solve. They demonstrated that projects wanted better ways to select market makers, structure engagements and understand performance.

We simply had a different thesis around how those products should be delivered. Most notably, that critical infrastructure like MM monitoring and RFQs shouldn’t be locked behind SaaS paywalls or expensive advisory engagements.

And I don’t think any of this needs to be zero-sum.

There is plenty of room for multiple companies to build great products in the same category.

Personally, I’d rather spend our time shipping better software than publicly tearing down other builders.

If another platform develops a better methodology, feature, dataset or product, that should motivate us to improve ours. That’s how competition is supposed to work.

And we’re building well beyond market maker analytics. MM monitoring and RFQs are only one part of Forgd.

We’ve expanded the platform into tokenomics and protocol design, exchange listing intelligence, token unlock tracking, market structure analytics and novel institutional-grade research.

These problems are interconnected, and we ultimately think better data leads to better decisions throughout a token’s lifecycle.

5. I’ll end with a question.

What actually makes someone the “best” market maker?

- Is it the desk that consistently provides the most depth?
- The most maker volume?
- The tightest spreads?
- The strongest contractual KPI adherence?
- The best treasury management capabilities?
- The broadest exchange coverage?
- The projects with the best post-TGE price performance?
- Something else entirely?

@mdudas and anyone else who spends time thinking about market structure — I’d genuinely love to hear how you’d approach it. cc @hosseeb @BrianInCrypto @ahboyash 

Our leaderboard will continue to evolve as the dataset grows and we get better feedback.

The goal isn’t to declare that we’ve created the definitive answer to “Who is the best market maker?” The goal is to take one of the biggest black boxes in crypto and make it a little more transparent, measurable and data-driven.

We’ll keep publishing the methodology, listening to constructive criticism, improving the product, and letting the data speak for itself.

With this observation, Erika Masako Welch, Chief Content Officer of @LucidityInsight, explores how sovereign cloud becomes a strategic priority as governments and businesses confront their dependence on digital infrastructure.

In her analysis, Welch describes two forces driving this shift: geopolitical tensions that raise concerns over foreign access to data and infrastructure, and AI's growing role in building and running online services. For organizations that rely on cloud platforms to operate, control over that infrastructure becomes a boardroom issue.

At the center is the DFINITY Foundation's (@dfinity) Internet Computer, an open network that combines computing resources across data centers to host software and data. Its cloud engines allow organizations to choose the hardware supporting their services and change that configuration as their needs evolve.

Welch highlights founder Dominic Williams' claim that enterprises can move from hyperscaler computing resources to dedicated hardware in their home countries “without interrupting or even degrading the services you are running.”

text:

这位30年几乎没有出现过年度亏损、做过索罗斯旗下基金操盘手的投资大佬，在X上异常低调 @standuquesne ，但有个加密玩家们喜闻乐见的投资理论，那就是：

“先上车，在研究”。

@BTCdayu 大宇老师的公众号在5个月前，曾系统的整理了德鲁肯米勒公开的访谈和各类投资发言，其中就提到了这一点，原文是这么说的：
------
“德鲁肯米勒自己更通俗地表述为“Buy first, analyze later”。

逻辑是这样的：“市场是聪明的、很快的，而且因为通讯和技术，越来越快。如果我听到一个我喜欢的想法，去花两三个月去分析它，我可能会错过大部分行情，然后心理上被瘫痪——一个 100 块的股票你看着它涨到 160，即使你知道它会到 400，你的脑子也会卡住，等回调。”

所以他的做法是，先建一个有意义但不致命的仓位（比如 1–2% NAV 的探索仓，看好的话才扩到 20–25%），然后开始真正做研究。

如果发现自己错了，就卖掉；如果对了，就金字塔加仓。

NVIDIA 那笔交易就是经典案例。

他后来回忆，早在 2022 年前后，他的年轻分析师就不断提醒他：Stanford、MIT 一类顶尖工程师的兴趣，正在从 crypto 转向 AI。这是第一个信号。

当时他并没有真正理解英伟达在 AI 里的位置，仍大致把它看成一家游戏显卡公司；但他听完团队说“这就是 AI 最直接的表达式”后，先买了一笔不算大的仓位。

不久后，ChatGPT 发布。他后来承认：“那纯粹是运气。”更准确地说，NVDA 当时已经从 2021 年三百多美元的高点跌到 2022 年底约 150 美元附近，”。

他先建仓，之后才真正开始深入研究。这正是索罗斯的那条老规则——先投资，再调查。”
-----
